title: One semisimple torus element detects the whole scheme centralizer
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups below are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$, and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. A torus is a group scheme $T$ isomorphic over $k$ to $(\mathbf G_m)^r$ for some integer $r\geq0$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $G$ be smooth and connected, and let $T\subseteq G$ be a torus. A point $s\in G(k)$ is semisimple if its image in every finite-dimensional algebraic representation $G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is diagonalizable; here $V$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is its group scheme of invertible linear maps, and an algebraic representation is a homomorphism of group schemes. There exists a semisimple point $s\in T(k)$ with the following property for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and every $g\in G(A)$: $$gs_A=s_Ag\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g_{A\prime}t=tg_{A\prime}\text{ for every commutative }A\text{-algebra }A\prime\text{ and every }t\in T(A\prime).$$ Here $s_A$ denotes scalar extension of $s$. Thus the centralizer functors of $s$ and of $T$ agree on all algebras, including nonreduced ones.

source.place: Lemma 16.42 and its proof, printed p.339: a faithful representation and separation of its finitely many torus weights. The conclusion is equality of centralizer schemes, not just equality on field-valued points.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sc-kernel-subgroup] to $\mathrm{id}_G$: its kernel is the identity subgroup $1\subseteq G$, which is normal since $\{1\}$ is normal in every $G(A)$. Apply [lem-sfb-normal-subgroup-representation-kernel] with $N=1$. This gives $n\geq1$ and a representation $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_{n,k}$ with kernel $1$ on every commutative $k$-algebra. Thus every $\rho_A$ is injective: $\rho_A(x)=\rho_A(y)$ implies $\rho_A(xy^{-1})=I_n$, hence $xy^{-1}=1$. Put $V=k^n$. Affineness and finite type are exactly the hypotheses of the representation-kernel lemma.

source.place: Lemma 16.42, first sentence, printed p.339; Corollary 5.19, printed p.103, applied to the identity subgroup (an alternative to Theorem 4.9, printed p.87).

proof.text: Restrict $\rho$ to $T$; this is a homomorphism $T\to\mathrm{GL}_{n,k}=\operatorname{GL}(V)$, $V=k^n$. Apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-representation-weight-decomposition]: $V=\bigoplus_{\chi\in\Omega}V_\chi$ for a finite set $\Omega$ of pairwise distinct characters $\chi:T\to\mathbf G_m$ with $V_\chi\ne0$, where $\rho_B(t)(v\otimes1)=v\otimes\chi_B(t)$ for $v\in V_\chi$, every commutative $k$-algebra $B$ and every $t\in T(B)$. Concatenate bases of the $V_\chi$ to a basis of $V$. By the same node, in the induced $B$-basis of $V\otimes_kB$ the matrix of $\rho_B(t)$ is block diagonal with scalar block $\chi_B(t)I$, for every $B$ and every $t\in T(B)$. From now on write matrices in this basis: the change of basis is conjugation by one matrix in $\mathrm{GL}_n(k)$, so it commutes with every scalar extension and keeps the injectivity of step 1.

source.place: Lemma 16.42 and Theorem 12.12(a)--(d), printed pp.339 and 234--235.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-torus-finite-character-separation] to this finite character set $\Omega$, obtaining $s\in T(k)$ with pairwise distinct scalars $\lambda_\chi=\chi_k(s)$. This point is semisimple in the precise sense of the item. Indeed, for any finite-dimensional algebraic representation $\eta:G\to\mathrm{GL}(W)$, apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-representation-weight-decomposition] to $\eta|_T$. With $B=k$ and $t=s$ it says that, in a basis of $W$ concatenated from bases of its weight spaces, $\eta_k(s)$ is diagonal with entries $\psi_k(s)$; for $W=0$ there is nothing to show. No separation condition on the weights of $W$ is necessary.

source.place: Lemma 16.42, character-equality loci and semisimplicity, printed p.339; Theorem 12.12, printed p.235.

proof.text: Fix a commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and $g\in G(A)$ with $gs_A=s_Ag$. Write $M=\rho_A(g)$ in the weight basis, using the pointwise matrix interpretation in [def-sc-general-linear-group]. Since $\rho_A(s_A)$ has scalar block $\lambda_\chi I$, its commutation with $M$ gives $$(\lambda_\psi-\lambda_\chi)M_{\chi\psi}=0.$$ For $\chi\ne\psi$ the scalar difference is nonzero in $k$, hence has an inverse in $k$ whose image in $A$ is an inverse. Multiplying by it gives $M_{\chi\psi}=0$. Thus $M$ is block diagonal. Over any commutative $A$-algebra $B$, these zero blocks stay zero, while $\rho_B(t)$ for $t\in T(B)$ is scalar on each block by step 2. Block multiplication gives $\rho_B(g_B)\rho_B(t)=\rho_B(t)\rho_B(g_B)$. Injectivity of $\rho_B$ from step 1 gives $g_Bt=tg_B$. This computation also applies when $A$ or $B$ is the zero ring.

source.place: Lemma 16.42, weight-preserving centralizer argument, printed p.339; the displayed block equations supply its arbitrary-algebra refinement.

proof.text: Conversely, if $g_B$ commutes with every $t\in T(B)$ for every commutative $A$-algebra $B$, take $B=A$ with its identity structure map and $t=s_A$. This gives $gs_A=s_Ag$. Together with step 4 this is the required equivalence, for the single point $s$ fixed in step 3 and for every $A,g$. The identities are natural under change of algebra because $s_A$ and the group homomorphisms are scalar extensions. Hence the two centralizer functors agree, including on nonreduced algebras. For the rank-zero torus the only character is trivial, so all blocks coalesce and $s=1$ works.

source.place: Lemma 16.42, concluding equality of centralizers, printed p.339; direct functor-of-points verification.

proof_origin.place: Lemma 16.42, printed p.339: weight-separation route, with the final field-points/smoothness argument replaced by the explicit block calculation over every algebra; faithful representation obtained from Corollary 5.19.

Sources checked: Milne iAG2017 Lemma 16.42 with its proof (p.339) and Theorem 12.12 with Remark 12.13 (pp.234-235). The item statement is unchanged from the base (compared against about 60 earlier run snapshots) and no other group has split it. The route matches Milne: a faithful representation, torus weights, and a point s outside the finitely many loci where two characters agree. Milne's final smoothness/k-points step (13.8) is replaced by a block-matrix computation over every algebra A. That computation is correct: the scalar differences lie in k^x, so they stay units in A (including A=0), and injectivity of rho_B on B-points closes it. Step 5 (the converse) is correct and fixes s before A and g. The new separation node is true and is not a restatement of the item: each nontrivial character is a monomial x^m with m nonzero, and the complement of finitely many proper closed loci has a point because k is infinite. Small cases checked: r=0, an empty set, a single character, and 1, t, t^p in characteristic p (every t in F_p fails by Fermat, but k infinite gives a good t). It is false over a finite field (t and t^q agree on F_q^x), so the algebraically closed hypothesis is needed. One fault, repaired (C7/C3-type): steps 2 and 3 took the weight decomposition of a G_m^r-representation from a side clause of the unsplit lem-sfb-torus-coherent-fixed-point-formula, instantiated with H=T and Z=Spec k. That node is an agent-formulated fixed-point theorem whose sources (Nielsen, Iversen) are WANTED, while Milne 12.12, which Lemma 16.42 itself cites, gives the fact directly. The DAG has no rank-r version: gm-representation-weight-basis is rank 1 only, character-eigenspaces-independent gives independence but not spanning, and central-torus-faithful-weight-blocks builds its own representation.
